blindSummary:
This state/province hosts the most trans-visible public space in the country: an established transgender monastic order fielded one of its highest-ranking monks — at the head of 15 trans spiritual leaders — in ceremonial bathing at the world's largest religious gathering (January–February 2025), a place secured within the broader monastic governance system through organising that began in 2015. A trans visitor at this festival stands inside an institutionally recognised religious hierarchy, not a marginalised underground. The inclusion is contested: a rival leadership instalment drew protests from within the community and other sects, some senior figures threatened to boycott the next edition a dozen years out, and a top-ranking trans monk who objected was physically attacked on 12 February 2025. A transgender welfare board has been constituted here.

The recognition is visitor-facing and institutionally validated, but seasonally concentrated and unsettled — the festival-week attack and boycott threats show an ongoing contest rather than settled protection. A lone strangulation of a trans woman during a robbery in a major industrial city (August 2025) is recorded without a patterned response and does not constitute a regional finding. What this state/province lacks relative to the country's most institutionalised examples is any comprehensive policy framework or judicial endorsement, and relative to another large state it avoids the religion-screened festival entry that creates outing mechanisms at public gatherings. The net positive is narrow and temporally concentrated.

The government's official press portal, upper-house reply (8 Dec 2021, the responsible minister): 12 of the country's states/provinces and centrally administered territories had constituted transgender welfare boards under the 2020 national rules; this state/province is among the 12.
